result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Categorical Outcomes: Nominal or Ordered?" subtitle: "Choosing the model family · cumulative proportions · why not linear · sparse categories · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Regression workshop: continuous (linear) and **binary** (logistic) outcomes - Today: outcomes with **three or more categories**: anaemia severity, place of delivery, BP stage, disease stage - By the end you can: - say whether an outcome is **nominal** or **ordered**, and why it matters - read **cumulative proportions** - explain why **linear regression** and **dichotomising** are poor choices - spot **sparse categories** ::: ## Our data: a maternal health survey ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **1,500 women** with a birth in the last 3 years (synthetic, built like an NFHS-type survey) - **Anaemia** in four **ordered** levels: None < Mild < Moderate < Severe - **Place of delivery** in four **unordered** levels: Home, PHC, Public hospital, Private hospital - Predictors: wealth quintile, education, residence, tribal group, antenatal visits, BMI, parity, age ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mat |> select(id, age, education, wealth, tribal, anc_visits, anaemia, delivery) |> head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 id age education wealth tribal anc_visits anaemia delivery 1 W0001 23 None 2 No 2 Moderate Public hospital 2 W0002 28 Secondary 4 No 4 None Private hospital 3 W0003 27 Secondary 2 No 3 Mild Public hospital 4 W0004 25 Secondary 3 Yes 7 None Public hospital 5 W0005 30 Primary 2 Yes 3 Severe Home 6 W0006 17 None 3 No 5 None Public hospital ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Which type of outcome? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Nominal or ordered? | Outcome | Type | Model family | |---|---|---| | Hypertension yes/no | binary | logistic | | **Anaemia: none, mild, moderate, severe** | **ordered** | **ordinal logistic** (proportional odds) | | **Place of delivery** | **nominal** | **multinomial logistic** | | Cases per month | count | Poisson / negative binomial | | Time to death | time-to-event | Cox | ::: {.key} Ask: **does the order of the categories mean something?** Mild anaemia is *between* none and moderate, so anaemia is ordered. "PHC" is not between "Home" and "Public hospital" in any statistical sense, so delivery place is nominal. ::: ## Cumulative proportions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(100 * prop.table(table(mat$anaemia)), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None Mild Moderate Severe 54.4 26.5 12.2 6.9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(100 * cumsum(prop.table(table(mat$anaemia))), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None Mild Moderate Severe 54.4 80.9 93.1 100.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - The second line is **P(Y ≤ k)**: **81%** of women have *mild anaemia or better* - The proportional-odds model (Session 2) models the **log odds of these cumulative probabilities** - Nominal outcomes have no cumulative scale: each category is compared with a **reference** ::: # Topic 2 — Describing {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Anaemia by wealth ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(100 * prop.table(table(mat$wealth, mat$anaemia), 1), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None Mild Moderate Severe 1 29.6 32.7 20.8 16.9 2 41.3 36.9 14.2 7.7 3 59.3 23.7 11.4 5.7 4 69.1 20.8 7.3 2.8 5 78.2 14.5 6.7 0.6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(mat, aes(factor(wealth), fill = anaemia)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", direction = -1) + labs(x = "Wealth quintile (1 = poorest)", y = "Proportion", fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_categorical_outcomes_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} The share with **no anaemia** rises from about 30% to 78%, and **severe** anaemia almost vanishes in the richest quintile. A **100% stacked bar** is the standard picture for an ordered outcome. ::: # Topic 3 — What not to do {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Treating categories as numbers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(lm(as.numeric(anaemia) ~ wealth, data = mat))["wealth"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` wealth -0.2395462 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.bad} - **Equal spacing** assumed: None to Mild is treated like Moderate to Severe - "-0.24 categories per quintile" is **not interpretable** and can be misleading at the extremes ::: ## Dichotomising ::: {.warn} Collapsing to "any anaemia vs none" **throws away** the difference between mild and severe, loses **power**, and depends on **where you cut**. Use it for a simple summary, not as the analysis when the ordering is available. ::: ## Checklist before modelling ::: {.good} 1. **Nominal or ordered?** (order meaningful?) 2. **Counts per category**: the smallest has about 103 women here; very small categories (a few per cent or fewer than about 10 per predictor) make estimates unstable: **merge** neighbouring categories if it makes clinical sense 3. **Reference category** (nominal): choose one that is **large and meaningful** (Home) 4. Plan the **assumption check** (proportional odds) ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `ordinal-workshop/labs/lab1_outcomes.R` - levels, percentages and **cumulative** percentages - 100% stacked bars by wealth - the wrong model (linear on 1-4) and sparse-category check ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a380bk.h0q6ed" data-show="QW5hZW1pYSBncmFkZWQgbm9uZSwgbWlsZCwgbW9kZXJhdGUgb3Igc2V2ZXJl" data-explain="T25seSBmb3IgYW5hZW1pYSBncmFkZSBkbyB0aGUgY2F0ZWdvcmllcyBoYXZlIGEgbmF0dXJh bCwgbWVhbmluZ2Z1bCBvcmRlci4gVGhlIG90aGVycyBhcmUgdW5vcmRlcmVkIGxhYmVscywg c28gYSBub21pbmFsIG1vZGVsIGlzIG5lZWRlZC4="} Which outcome is ordered, and so suited to an ordinal model? - Place of delivery: home, PHC, or a hospital - Blood group: A, B, AB or O in the patient - Anaemia graded none, mild, moderate or severe - Religion recorded in the survey of households ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a38dk8.h0qkvp" data-show="ODElIG9mIHdvbWVuIGhhdmUgbm8gb3IgbWlsZCBhbmFlbWlh" data-explain="QSBjdW11bGF0aXZlIHByb3BvcnRpb24gYWRkcyB0aGUgbG93ZXIgY2F0ZWdvcmllczogTm9u ZSAoNTQlKSBwbHVzIE1pbGQgKDI3JSkgaXMgODElLCB0aGUgcHJvYmFiaWxpdHkgb2YgbWls ZCBvciBiZXR0ZXIu"} The cumulative percentages for anaemia are 54, 81, 93 and 100. What does 81 mean? - 81% of women have mild anaemia - 81% of women have no or mild anaemia - 81% of women have at least mild anaemia - The odds of mild anaemia are 81 ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a38qsy.h0qzd3" data-show="SXQgYXNzdW1lcyBlcXVhbCBnYXBzIGJldHdlZW4gdGhlIGNhdGVnb3JpZXMgaW4gc2V2ZXJp dHk=" data-explain="Q29kaW5nIGNhdGVnb3JpZXMgYXMgMSwgMiwgMywgNCBhc3N1bWVzIHRoZSBnYXAgYmV0d2Vl biBlYWNoIHBhaXIgaXMgdGhlIHNhbWUsIGFuZCBhbiBhdmVyYWdlIGNhdGVnb3J5IG51bWJl ciBoYXMgbm8gY2xlYXIgbWVhbmluZy4="} A linear regression of anaemia coded 1 to 4 on wealth is a poor choice because it... - It cannot produce a coefficient for wealth from the data supplied - It needs a much smaller number of women than the other models do - It assumes equal gaps between the categories in severity - It always gives a larger p-value for wealth than ordinal models do ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a3941o.h0rduh" data-show="SXQgZGlzY2FyZHMgdGhlIG1pbGQtc2V2ZXJlIGRpZmZlcmVuY2UgYW5kIGxvc2VzIHBvd2Vy " data-explain="Q29sbGFwc2luZyBjYXRlZ29yaWVzIHRocm93cyBhd2F5IGluZm9ybWF0aW9uIG9uIHNldmVy aXR5LCByZWR1Y2VzIHByZWNpc2lvbiwgYW5kIHRoZSByZXN1bHQgZGVwZW5kcyBvbiB0aGUg Y2hvc2VuIGN1dC1wb2ludC4="} What is the main cost of dichotomising an ordered outcome into 'any anaemia' vs 'none'? - It makes the outcome nominal and so impossible to model at all - It requires the outcome data to be normally distributed in each group - It changes the direction of the effect in the very large majority of data sets - It discards the mild-severe difference and loses power ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="a39haa.h0rsbr" data-show="VGhhdCBubyBjYXRlZ29yeSBpcyBzbyBzbWFsbCB0aGF0IGVzdGltYXRlcyBiZWNvbWUgdW5z dGFibGU=" data-explain="VmVyeSBzbWFsbCBjYXRlZ29yaWVzIG1ha2UgY29lZmZpY2llbnRzIHVuc3RhYmxlIGFuZCB0 ZXN0cyB1bnJlbGlhYmxlOyBjb25zaWRlciBtZXJnaW5nIG5laWdoYm91cmluZyBjYXRlZ29y aWVzIHdoZW4gaXQgaXMgY2xpbmljYWxseSBzZW5zaWJsZS4="} What should you check about the categories of an outcome before fitting a model? - That no category is so small that estimates become unstable - That the categories are listed in alphabetical order by name - That every category has exactly the same number of women in it - That the outcome is stored in the data file as a number ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Ordered or nominal?** decides the model family - Ordered: **cumulative proportions**, 100% stacked bars - Do not code categories as 1-4 in **linear regression**; avoid needless **dichotomising** - Check **sparse categories** and choose a sensible **reference** (nominal) ::: **Next:** Session 2: ordinal logistic regression

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
